text: Education begins with stories, since children hear stories before they undertake the training of the body (Republic II, 377a-b). For that reason the founders of the city must supervise the makers of stories, and Socrates gives Glaucon two laws for speech about the gods. The first is that God is good, and therefore “not the cause of all things” but only of good things (Republic II, 379b-c). Since the evils in the world far outnumber the goods, some other cause must be found for them, because nothing good can be harmful (Republic II, 379c). The second law is that God neither changes nor deceives. Whatever is in the best condition is least altered by outside forces, and a perfect being would not willingly exchange itself for something worse (Republic II, 380d-381c). Hence Homer’s two jars on the threshold of Zeus must go, as must the poet who makes a god responsible for the ruin of a household and the old stories in which gods alter their shapes (Republic II, 379d-383c). The lie most hated by gods and human beings is not the lie spoken aloud but the lie in the soul: to be deceived about reality in the most important part of oneself. A god has no such lie within, and no motive to put such a lie in anyone else (Republic II, 382a-e).
